# Just enough data handling

::: {.callout-note}
## Video
Coming soon.
:::

**In this chapter:** make a new column, pick out some rows, and summarise by group.

Data rarely arrive in exactly the form you need. These few tools cover most simple jobs.

```{r}
morph <- read.csv("data/morphometry.csv")
```

## Change or add a column

Heights and lengths are in millimetres. Convert them to centimetres by dividing by 10:

```{r}
morph$Height <- morph$Height / 10
morph$HandLength <- morph$HandLength / 10
head(morph)
```

Assigning to an existing column (`morph$Height <-`) replaces it. Assigning to a new name adds a column.

## Pick out rows

`subset()` keeps the rows that meet a condition. Note the double equals sign `==`, which means "is equal to".

```{r}
females <- subset(morph, Sex == "Female")
nrow(females)
```

`nrow()` counts the rows. Text values such as `"Female"` need quotes; numbers do not. A single `=` instead of `==` gives an error, and is one of the most common mistakes.

Other conditions: `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` and `!=` (is not equal to).

```{r}
tall <- subset(morph, Height > 180)
nrow(tall)
```

## Summarise

```{r}
mean(morph$Height)
sd(morph$Height)
```

## Summarise by group

`tapply()` applies a function to a column, separately for each group:

```{r}
tapply(morph$Height, morph$Sex, mean)
tapply(morph$Height, morph$Sex, sd)
```

Read it as: take `Height`, split it by `Sex`, and give the `mean` of each part. The result is one number per group, labelled with the group name.

## Functions in this chapter

- `subset()`: keep the rows that meet a condition.
- `nrow()`: count rows.
- `mean()`, `sd()`: mean and standard deviation.
- `tapply()`: apply a function separately to each group.

## Your turn

Import `chirps.csv`. Make a new column `tempC` with the temperature in °C, using `(temperature - 32) / 1.8`. How many rows have more than 17 chirps per second? What is the mean `tempC` for those rows?
